outcome: No source I could reach records a settlement, a partial result on the converse, or a move in the counterexample bounds for the Agoh–Giuga congruence since 26 January 2024: no composite n is reported to satisfy nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n), no counterexample is known, and the best published counterexample bound I found is the 2013/2014 figure of 19,908 digits. The in-window items are a reformulation of the converse as non-existence of odd Giuga numbers (Svinin, arXiv:2607.18607, July 2026), a Lean proof produced by DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus of the Carmichael characterisation for the neighbouring OEIS A309132 function (repository, May 2026), a Lean-checked lemma that strong Giuga numbers are Carmichael (linked October 2026), and an unrefereed mailing-list test on a different power sum (Rotondo, September 2026).
problem_asks: (1) Forward direction: for every prime p, p·B_{p−1} ≡ −1 (mod p). Known from von Staudt–Clausen and Fermat, per Wikipedia and OEIS A046094. (2) Converse: if an integer p > 1 satisfies p·B_{p−1} ≡ −1 (mod p), then p is prime; equivalently, no composite n satisfies nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n). Even composites fail trivially because B_{n−1} = 0 for even n ≥ 4, so the open content lies in odd composites. The statement names only the Bernoulli-number form. Giuga's 1950 power-sum form (sum of k^{n−1} for k = 1..n−1 is ≡ −1 mod n), the Carmichael/Giuga-number reduction and the counterexample size bounds are not asked for by the bullet; they are recorded as context because Kellner (2004) shows the two forms are one conjecture.

events.what_happened: Bernd C. Kellner, 'The Equivalence of Giuga's and Agoh's Conjectures', arXiv:math/0409259 (math.NT), one version. Gives a direct proof that Giuga's power-sum congruence and Agoh's Bernoulli congruence are equivalent, and derives from the argument a combined conjecture written as a sum of fractions. Per search excerpts of the paper, the difference of the two sums mod n is n/2 when n ≡ 2 (mod 4), n > 2, and 0 otherwise, and Agoh had established the connection in 1993. Agoh's Bernoulli form is attributed to Agoh's 1990 formulation, published in Manuscripta Mathematica in 1995 (Wikipedia); sources differ on 1990 versus 1995.
events.revisions: One version (v1, 15 Sep 2004); no later revisions listed on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Shows the power-sum form and the Bernoulli form of the conjecture are equivalent for each n (as far as the abstract and search excerpts show), so the two named forms are one conjecture. Establishes no instance of either congruence for a composite n.
events.remains: The converse of both forms: that no composite n satisfies the congruence.
events.directly_checkable: The equivalence is an algebraic identity, not an object. Either congruence can be tested for any given n by computing B_{n−1} mod n.
events.direction: Neutral on the converse. Confirms that the two forms in circulation name one conjecture.
people: Takashi Agoh (Bernoulli form, 1990 formulation / 1995 publication, and 1993 connection as cited by Kellner)
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0409259 (opened: abstract and metadata only; main theorem read from search excerpts)
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1305.1867 (Meštrović; cited for the equivalence; search excerpt only)

events.what_happened: D. Borwein, J. M. Borwein, P. B. Borwein and R. Girgensohn, 'Giuga's Conjecture on Primality', American Mathematical Monthly 103 (1996), 40–50 (JSTOR 2975213 per ProofWiki; not opened). Shows that any composite counterexample n must have at least 3459 distinct prime factors and so at least about 13,800 decimal digits (Wikipedia gives 13,800; Grau and Oller-Marcén, arXiv:1103.3483, give 13,887 from the 3459-prime figure). Earlier bounds from Giuga (1950, at least 1000 digits) and E. Bedocchi (1700 digits, date not established) are cited in the same literature. Wikipedia also cites Sorini (2001) with a bound of 10^36067, which I could not check against Sorini's paper.
events.delivers: A lower bound on any counterexample to the congruence: at least 3459 distinct prime factors and about 13,800 digits, where a counterexample is a composite n that is both Carmichael and Giuga. Bounds the size of a hypothetical object; establishes no non-existence.
events.remains: Whether any composite counterexample exists at all.

events.doubts: The digit figure differs between sources (13,800 versus 13,887). Sorini's 10^36067 bound, as cited by Wikipedia, is far larger than the 2013 figure and is probably for a restricted method; not checked.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture. Makes a counterexample computationally implausible but does not rule one out.

events.what_happened: José María Grau and Antonio M. Oller-Marcén, 'Generalizing Giuga's conjecture', arXiv:1103.3483 (2011; month inferred from arXiv number). Introduces the congruences sum_{j=1}^{n−1} j^{k(n−1)} ≡ −1 (mod n) for each k and studies which composite n satisfy them (search excerpt of the follow-up arXiv:1311.3522: for composite n the congruence holds iff n is a Giuga number and λ(n)/gcd(λ(n), n−1) divides k). The paper lists open questions: whether odd Giuga numbers exist, whether there are infinitely many Giuga numbers, whether Lava's arithmetic-derivative conjecture holds, and conjectures that certain k-generalised sets are empty for k = 2, 3, 5.
events.revisions: Related: 'On a variant of Giuga numbers' (arXiv:1103.3428, Grau–Luca–Oller-Marcén, Acta Math. Sinica 2012, search excerpt only); journal version of 1103.3483 in JIS vol. 15 (2012), search link only, not opened.
events.delivers: Generalises the k = 1 congruence (the power-sum form of the bullet) to exponent k(n−1). Gives partial characterisations for k ≥ 2 and restates open questions. For k = 1 it establishes nothing new.
events.remains: The k = 1 case, which is the bullet's congruence in power-sum form.
events.doubts: The reader rendered the Agoh form as 'n B_n ≡ −1 (mod n)', with the index n instead of n−1. This may be a transcription error of my reader or a slip in the paper; not checked against the PDF.
events.direction: Generalisation. Neutral on the k = 1 case.

events.what_happened: Andrei Vieru, 'Agoh's conjecture: its generalizations, its analogues', arXiv:1107.2938 (math.NT; v1 14 Jul 2011, v2 26 Jul 2011, v3 16 May 2012). The abstract, as I read it, says the paper formulates two generalizations of Agoh's conjecture (with a parameter q, where q = 1 is Agoh's case), congruence conjectures involving hyperbolic functions and Nörlund numbers, and a thesis about combinatorial objects. A search excerpt instead says one generalisation is proved, in terms of the arithmetic derivative. I could not read the body.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jul 2011; v2 26 Jul 2011; v3 16 May 2012 (current, per arXiv history).
events.delivers: Generalisations of Agoh's congruence with a parameter q. The q = 1 case is the conjecture itself, so these results say nothing about it. If the search excerpt is right that one generalisation is proved, that proof concerns a changed question (general q), not q = 1.
events.remains: The conjecture at q = 1, i.e. the bullet's statement.
events.doubts: The abstract says 'formulate' and the search excerpt says 'proves one'. The body was not read, so it is unresolved whether any part is proved.
events.direction: Conjectural generalisations. No direction on the q = 1 case.

events.what_happened: Thomas Sauvaget, 'Remarks on an interpolation between Wilson's theorem and Giuga's conjecture', arXiv:1911.09492 (2019; month inferred from the arXiv number). Builds a family of congruences H_k(n) that interpolates between Wilson's theorem (k = 1, a proved characterisation of primes) and Giuga's (k = n−1). Proves partial results (H_k(p) ≡ 0 mod p for primes and suitable k; H_k(n) ≡ 1 mod n for composite squarefree n with k ≤ n/2). The general characterisation (Conjecture 2) and Conjecture 3 are unproved. The appendix reports that Conjecture 4 is false, per the referees. The paper describes the family as a possible approach to Giuga's conjecture, and Remark 6 says a cancellation modulo the largest prime factor would yield a contradiction; that cancellation is not established.
events.delivers: Partial congruence results and a reformulation (the case k = n−1 is Giuga's conjecture). The k = 1 Wilson characterisation is classical. Nothing settles the composite-nonexistence part of the bullet.
events.remains: All of the bullet's converse: no composite n with nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n).
events.doubts: The author's own Conjecture 4 is reported false in the appendix. The proposed approach depends on an unproven cancellation (Remark 6). Conjecture 3 is supported only by numerical data.

events.what_happened: OEIS A309132: a(n) is the denominator of F(n) = A027641(n−1)/n + A027642(n−1)/n², where A027641 and A027642 are the numerator and denominator of the Bernoulli numbers. Entry and comments from 14 July 2019. Thomas Ordowski's conjecture: for n > 1, a(n) = 1 iff n is prime. Jonathan Sondow's Theorem 1 (14 Jul 2019): a(p) = 1 for primes p, via von Staudt–Clausen. Amiram Eldar (16 Jul 2019): checked the conjecture to n = 101101. Sondow's Theorem 2 (19 Jul 2019): for prime or Carmichael n, a(n) is the denominator of the sum over primes p | n of 1/p minus 1/n. Ordowski's 'Carmichael conjecture' (15 Jul 2019): composite n with squarefree a(n) are exactly the Carmichael numbers. The OEIS page asks: 'Is this conjecture equivalent to the Agoh–Giuga conjecture?', with no answer on the page.
events.revisions: OEIS comments from 14 Jul to 16 Aug 2019; 2026 comments added (see the AlphaProof Nexus event). Page last modified 11 Oct 2026.
events.delivers: The prime case of the criterion a(n) = 1 iff n prime (Sondow, Theorem 1), a Bernoulli-denominator reformulation, and a finite check to 101101. Nothing for composite n. The Carmichael conjecture it records was later proved (see the AlphaProof Nexus event).
events.remains: Whether any composite n has a(n) = 1, i.e. the converse of the a(n) = 1 criterion, and whether that criterion is equivalent to Agoh–Giuga (asked, not answered, on the OEIS page).

checked_by.qualification: OEIS contributor who computes sequence terms
checked_by.what_they_did: Computed a(n) and checked the primality conjecture up to n = 101101

events.directly_checkable: a(n) can be computed for any given n from B_{n−1}, so the finite check is directly reproducible.
events.doubts: The equivalence to Agoh–Giuga is asked, not answered. The Carmichael conjecture here was proved in 2026 by an AI-driven Lean proof (see that event).
events.direction: Proves the prime half of the a(n) = 1 criterion and conjectures the converse. The converse, if true, would make a(n) = 1 an exact primality test, which is the content of the bullet's converse only if the equivalence to Agoh–Giuga holds.

events.what_happened: Takashi Agoh, 'A Note on Fermat's Congruence', INTEGERS 25 (2025), #A31. Accepted March 2025 and published 26 March 2025, per search excerpts. The Integers PDF is undecodable binary to my reader, so the content below is from search excerpts: it extends Fermat's congruence to a composite modulus nm, derives a congruence satisfied by primes and by Carmichael numbers, and applies this to twin prime and Sophie Germain prime characterisations (per the Wikipedia summary of Agoh's work). By the search summary, the congruence does not characterise primes because Carmichael numbers also satisfy it. This is an inference from the abstract.
events.delivers: A Fermat-type congruence satisfied by all primes and all Carmichael numbers, with applications to twin and Sophie Germain prime conditions. Not the Agoh–Giuga congruence, and by the search summary not a primality characterisation.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus produced a Lean proof of the statement that for all n, (n composite and a(n) squarefree) iff n is a Carmichael number, where a(n) is the OEIS A309132 function. The Lean file APNOutputs/OEIS/A309132_conjecture_carmichael.lean is in the public repository google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results, first committed 19 May 2026 with the message 'Results for AlphaProof Nexus' by aferr. The statement is the Carmichael conjecture credited to Thomas Ordowski (2019). The OEIS entry (comment by Ralf Stephan, 25 May 2026) says the proof 'was achieved by an autonomous AI agent' and credits AlphaProof Nexus. The paper arXiv:2605.22763 (Tsoukalas et al., 21 May 2026; v2 8 Jun 2026) reports that the agent proved 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures. Its statement formalisation step used Gemini to autoformalise the 492 OEIS statements (paper, Section 3). That paper's visible text does not name A309132; the attribution to this file rests on the repository.
events.revisions: Repository file committed 19 May 2026; arXiv:2605.22763 v1 21 May 2026, v2 8 Jun 2026; OEIS comment 25 May 2026.
events.delivers: For the A309132 function: a composite n has squarefree a(n) exactly when n is Carmichael. This does not say whether any composite n has a(n) = 1, the A309132 primality criterion. Since 1 is squarefree, the theorem confines any composite with a(n) = 1 to Carmichael numbers, which is already a standard restriction on Agoh–Giuga counterexamples, so it narrows nothing new about the bullet's congruence itself.
events.remains: Whether any composite n has a(n) = 1 (the converse of the A309132 criterion); whether that criterion is equivalent to nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n) (asked on the OEIS page, unanswered in the sources I read); the bullet's congruence itself.

events.what_happened: Andrei K. Svinin, 'On a certain arithmetic function defined via Bernoulli numbers', arXiv:2607.18607 (v1 21 Jul 2026; v2 5 Oct 2026). For odd n ≥ 3 defines χ(n) from the denominators of B_{n−1}/(n−1) and of B_{n−1} + 1/n. The formula, as transcribed by my reader from the HTML, is χ(n) = denom(B_{n−1}/(n−1)) / (n · denom(B_{n−1} + 1/n)). Theorem 1.6 (v2, per the reader): χ(n) is integer-valued iff n is prime or an odd Giuga number. The proof uses only von Staudt–Clausen and Korselt's criterion, with a case split on primes, composite non-Carmichael numbers and Carmichael numbers. The Conclusion says χ is integer-valued exactly for primes and for hypothetical counterexamples to Agoh–Giuga, and 'the existence of an odd Giuga number is equivalent to the negation of the Agoh-Giuga conjecture'. The paper says the non-existence of odd Giuga numbers is a fundamental open problem. The v1 abstract, as I read it, describes the function as unifying 'primes, Carmichael numbers, and Giuga numbers' and does not use 'odd'. The Introduction says any odd Giuga number, if one exists, is automatically Carmichael. Its Giuga numbers are the weak ones: a composite n with p | (n/p − 1) for every prime p | n.
events.revisions: v1 21 Jul 2026 (abstract names primes, Carmichael numbers, Giuga numbers); v2 5 Oct 2026 (Theorem 1.6 and Conclusion state odd n and odd Giuga numbers).
events.delivers: Two formulations of one question. Per Theorem 1.6, integrality of χ on odd n ≥ 3 holds exactly for primes and odd Giuga numbers. Per the Conclusion, the negation of Agoh–Giuga is equivalent to the existence of an odd Giuga number. This relies on the Introduction's claim that every odd Giuga number is Carmichael, which I could not verify (see doubts). It does not construct or exclude any odd Giuga number or composite solution.
events.remains: The bullet's converse, which by the paper's own equivalence reduces to non-existence of odd Giuga numbers. Whether any odd Giuga number exists. The forward direction is not in question.
events.directly_checkable: χ(n) can be computed for any given odd n from B_{n−1}. An odd Giuga number, if one were found, could be tested against the Giuga condition for each prime factor.
events.doubts: (1) The Conclusion's equivalence depends on the Introduction's claim that any odd Giuga number is Carmichael. The paper's Giuga numbers are the weak ones (p | n/p − 1). The only proof of an odd-Giuga-implies-Carmichael step I could find (Banks–Nevans–Pomerance; Giuga's counterexample characterisation) uses the strong notion (p²(p−1) | n − p), where p−1 | n−1 follows directly. For the weak notion, p | (n/p − 1) does not obviously give p−1 | n−1, so the step is unverified here. (2) The definition changed between v1 and v2 (v1: 'Giuga numbers'; v2: 'odd Giuga numbers'). I cannot tell whether v1 claimed the same theorem. (3) I read the HTML through a summarising reader, not the PDF; the formula and quotes are as that reader transcribed them. (4) No citation, comment or OEIS entry for this function found in the sources I checked.
events.direction: Reformulation. If its steps hold, it makes the bullet's converse equivalent to non-existence of odd Giuga numbers. It does not decide that either way.

events.what_happened: Davide Rotondo, SeqFan mailing-list post 'A New Discovery on Prime Numbers: A Test Based on Giuga Numbers' (10 Sep 2026), with replies on 11 Sep 2026. The post defines G(n) = sum of j^n for j = 1..n (exponent n, not n−1) and a triangle T(n,k) = G(n)/(G(k)·G(n−k)). It reports that for every prime n > 2 the reduced numerators in row n are divisible by n, checked up to n = 672; 2 fails, and 9 is the only composite that passes. Geoffrey Caveney (11 Sep) notes that the post's G(n) differs from the standard Giuga sum and asks that odd composites such as 15 be stated as failing (he checked 15 fails for k = 3). Rotondo (11 Sep) apologises and agrees with the point. Replies after the fourth message were not visible to my reader.
events.revisions: Posts of 10 and 11 Sep 2026; later replies not visible.
events.delivers: Nothing for the bullet. The test uses exponent n rather than n−1 and a different triangle. It asserts one direction (primes pass) over a finite range. It does not involve the congruence nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n).

disputes.summary: The Lean proof of the OEIS A309132 Carmichael characterisation is credited to Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus (repository google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results; OEIS comment of 25 May 2026), but MathWorld's Agoh's Conjecture page (updated 2 Oct 2026) cites 'Epoch AI (2026), LeanOpenProblems-results, accepted Lean submission for OEIS A309132'. I found no Epoch AI repository by that name, so it is unresolved whether there are two submissions or one mis-credited one.

The OEIS comment calls the A309132 proof 'achieved by an autonomous AI agent'. The DeepMind paper says 'the agent found proofs' for 44 OEIS conjectures, reports a manual review of their formalisations, and uses 'autonomously' only for the Erdős results. Whether the OEIS proofs were autonomous is not settled by the authors' own text I read.

Counterexample size bounds differ across sources: 13,800 digits (Borwein et al., 1996; Wikipedia), 13,887 digits from 3459 prime factors (Grau and Oller-Marcén), 19,907 digits (2013 seminar abstracts) and 19,908 digits (Skerritt, ICMS 2014). Sorini (2001), as cited by Wikipedia, gives 10^36067. These are not priority disputes, but a later pass should not mix them.

Svinin's v1 abstract describes the function's class as 'Giuga numbers'; v2 states the theorem and the equivalence for 'odd Giuga numbers'. The weak and strong Giuga definitions also differ (weak: p | n/p − 1; strong: n | 1 + Σ k^{n−1}), and the equivalence chain depends on which is meant.

summary: Sources checked: the Wikipedia article (last edited 1 Aug 2026), number.subwiki, MathWorld (updated 2 Oct 2026), OEIS A046094 (last modified 11 Oct 2026), and the Number wiki page ('The other direction is conjectural and open'), OEIS A309132 and A326579, the Formal Conjectures Lean file and its history, the lean-fc-proofs repository, the DeepMind AlphaProof Nexus repository and paper arXiv:2605.22763, the SeqFan threads, and the primary arXiv papers that I could open. On the Agoh–Giuga congruence itself nothing has changed: no composite n is reported to satisfy nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n), no counterexample is known, and every source I opened still calls the converse open. The closest in-window items are (a) Svinin's reformulation (arXiv:2607.18607, 21 Jul 2026, revised 5 Oct), which says integrality of an arithmetic function built from Bernoulli denominators holds exactly for primes and odd Giuga numbers, and that the negation of Agoh–Giuga is therefore equivalent to the existence of an odd Giuga number. No one has engaged with it, and its step 'every odd Giuga number is Carmichael' is unverified for the weak Giuga definition that the paper uses. (b) The AI-involved item: DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus produced a Lean proof (repository commit 19 May 2026) of the Carmichael characterisation for the OEIS A309132 function, that a composite n has squarefree a(n) exactly when n is Carmichael. This is an OEIS conjecture credited to Ordowski (2019). It is not the Agoh–Giuga statement: A309132's primality criterion (a(n) = 1 iff n prime) is conjecturally similar, and the OEIS page asks whether it is equivalent to Agoh–Giuga, but nothing I read answers that. (c) A Lean-checked lemma (linked 8 Oct 2026) that strong Giuga numbers are Carmichael, a standard reduction. (d) Rotondo's SeqFan test (10 Sep 2026) uses Σj^n rather than Σj^{n−1}, checks primes to 672 and gives no converse, so it does not bear on the congruence. (e) Agoh's 2025 Integers note on a Fermat-type congruence satisfied by primes and Carmichael numbers; I could not read the PDF. Before 2024, the bounds (Borwein et al. 1996, 13,800 digits; Skerritt 2013/2014, 19,908 digits) and the equivalence (Kellner 2004) stand, and the generalisations (Grau–Oller-Marcén 2011, Vieru 2011, Sauvaget 2019) give no progress on the k = 1 case. Where a call was close: first, whether the A309132 Carmichael theorem should count as moving the bullet's converse. I read it as a neighbouring reduction, since the restriction it gives is already standard for Agoh–Giuga counterexamples, and it does not decide whether a(n) = 1 can occur for composite n. Second, whether Svinin's paper is a substantive equivalence or only a restatement: its own Conclusion claims the former, but the odd-Giuga-implies-Carmichael step it relies on is unverified for the weak definition. Third, which AI attribution is right for the A309132 proof: MathWorld names an Epoch AI 'LeanOpenProblems-results' submission, the OEIS page and the DeepMind repository name AlphaProof Nexus, and I found no Epoch repository. AI involvement in the Agoh–Giuga congruence itself: no source I found credits any system with it. The Gemini autoformalisation of the 492 OEIS statements used in the DeepMind pipeline is a statement-formalisation step, not a proof, and I have recorded it in the summary only. Dataset-level counts are not mine to give.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the in-window items as partial progress: if A309132's criterion a(n) = 1 is exactly the Agoh congruence (Svinin's integrality formulation and the OEIS comments both point that way), then the AI-produced theorem restricts any composite counterexample to be Carmichael with a(n) = 1, and Svinin's Conclusion makes the converse equivalent to the non-existence of odd Giuga numbers. Read together, these move the structure of the converse, though not its status. The narrower reading, which I take, is that the AI-proved theorem is about squarefreeness and is a standard restriction, and that Svinin's equivalence is a restatement whose key step is unverified.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The arXiv PDF of 2607.18607, to read Theorem 1.6 and its proof, and in particular whether any odd weak Giuga number is shown to be Carmichael. (2) A short algebraic check of whether a(n) = 1 for a composite n is equivalent to nB_{n−1} ≡ −1 (mod n), which is the question the OEIS A309132 page asks. (3) Compiling APNOutputs/OEIS/A309132_conjecture_carmichael.lean, and reading the paper's list of the 44 OEIS results to see whether it is among them and whether the proofs were autonomous. (4) The Epoch AI 'LeanOpenProblems-results' repository that MathWorld cites, to see whether it is a second submission of the same statement. (5) The full text of Agoh's Integers 25 (2025) #A31 note, to confirm it does not address the Bernoulli congruence. (6) Any post-2013 computation of the counterexample bound, or the Integers 2013 PDF, to confirm the 19,908 figure is still the latest.

events.ai_basis: The agent found proofs for 44 conjectures that a manual review found to be correctly formalized and previously unproven.

events.credibility_reason: The equivalence relies on an unverified step (odd weak Giuga numbers are Carmichael), and the statement changed between v1 and v2; in any case it is a reformulation that settles nothing.
Finite check of a different sum (exponent n), with the author conceding a correction; it does not involve the stated congruence.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether nB_{n-1} ≡ -1 (mod n) characterises primes. The forward direction is classical and the converse is open. No event decides the converse. The only events that move a quantity on the problem are the counterexample-size lower bounds from 1996 and 2013, which are refereed and therefore digested; both predate the snapshot. The AlphaProof Nexus theorem proves Ordowski's Carmichael characterisation for the A309132 function. That is a different conjecture: the record says it is not known to be equivalent, and the restriction it gives is already standard. So it is a variant, and its AI credit is generated, from its own quote. Svinin's paper and the strong-Giuga-implies-Carmichael lemma are reformulations or known reductions, so both are none. Rotondo's test and Agoh's 2025 note concern different congruences, so both are variants.
judgement.doubts: The AlphaProof attribution is disputed: MathWorld credits an Epoch AI submission. The disagreement does not affect scope, since the event is a variant either way. The digit bounds differ across sources.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
